Social studies

The GED Social Studies test almost never asks for a date. It shows a document (a piece of the Constitution, a map, a graph, a speech, a political cartoon) and asks what it supports and what it does not. This course teaches exactly that, with real documents.

Topics 1 to 6 are ready: their eighteen lessons are linked below, each with a practice page. The other topics are being written now, in English and in Spanish; this page shows the whole plan.

How it is organized

  • One course, 24 lessons in 8 topics, about 4 hours of study each (about 96 hours in all). It is not split into levels.
  • Topics 1 and 2 build the tools (questioning sources and reading data); Topics 3 to 7 cover civics, history, economics, and geography in about the same proportion as the test, where civics and government weigh the most; Topic 8 puts everything together and prepares for test day.
  • The social studies practices of the GED (SSP.1 to SSP.11: drawing conclusions, central ideas, cause and effect, words in context, point of view, maps and graphs, fact and opinion, comparing sources, and data) appear in every topic. Each lesson shows the ones it works on, with their depth of knowledge (DOK) and the aligned CCR standards, and ends with GED-style questions.
  • Every question on the test joins one practice with one content topic: civics and government (about 50% of the test), U.S. history (20%), economics (15%), and geography and the world (15%).
  • When to take it: it leans on reading and argument more than on math. It works best after Reasoning through language arts Level 3 and Math Level 3, and it can go along with Language arts Level 4. Always start with Lesson 1.1.

Topic 1 Inquiry, sources, and analytical literacy

Source archive and extras

  • Source archive. The real public-domain documents the lessons use (the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, speeches, court decisions, and more). The English version links to each original as its official repository keeps it; the Spanish version adds a translation.
  • World history. An interactive timeline from prehistory to the 20th century, for reference.
  • Economics and geography. Interactive pages on supply and demand, the business cycle, the stock market, and the balance of payments, plus map work.
↑ Back to top

How each lesson works

  • Lesson and practice page. Each lesson has its own practice page with activities that make new exercises every time, linked by section.
  • Two tries. First wrong answer: a hint. Second: the solution, explained. Two-choice questions explain right away.
  • English and Spanish. Both versions are built from the same source, so they teach exactly the same thing.
  • GED and CCR standards at the end of each lesson, taken from the official GED Assessment Guide.
  • Accessible. Keyboard navigation, text descriptions for every figure, larger text and high contrast, and nothing to install.
  • Everything on LearnGED. No accounts, no outside sites: the readings, the tools, and the practice live here.
